source: Seoul National University Korean 2B, Unit 14 · 예의를 지켜요
pickEn: One exercise at a time — pick where to start.
hintKo: 숫자 키로 고르고, 화살표로 옮기고, Enter로 확인해요.

exercises.blurbEn: Pick the etiquette that fits each moment, and see it conjugated.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 알맞은 것을 골라 문장을 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Complete each sentence using the appropriate expression from the box, as in the example. (test)
exercises.noteEn: Each expression is used exactly once. Pick the dictionary form — the blank fills with the 해요 form the sentence actually needs.

items.en: When you drink with elders …
items.why: Drinking while facing an elder head-on reads as placing yourself on their level. You turn your head aside so the act is not done straight at them — the same instinct behind receiving with both hands.
items.grammar: 마시다 → 마셔요. The stem 마시- ends in ㅣ, and ㅣ + 어요 contracts to 셔요.

items.en: When you greet elders …
items.why: A greeting to an elder is carried by the bow, not by the words. 고개를 숙여서 is bowing the head, and -아/어서 links the two actions: you bow, and by bowing you greet.
items.grammar: 인사하다 → 인사해요. Every 하다 verb is irregular this way: 하 + 여요 → 해요. Note 께 in the prompt — it is the honorific of 에게/한테.

items.en: When you talk with someone you have just met …
items.why: With a person you have just met you do not yet know their age or standing, so 높임말 is the safe default. 반말 is for close friends or someone clearly younger — opening with it to a stranger is exactly the mistake this unit warns about.
items.grammar: 하다 → 해요. 높임말 and 존댓말 mean the same thing here; the textbook prints both, and the answer keeps just 높임말을 해요.

items.en: If an older person is on the bus …
items.why: Giving up your seat is the everyday form of 경로 우대, the senior-priority idea from this unit’s culture section.
items.grammar: 양보하다 → 양보해요. The prompt is already honorific twice over: 분 is the polite counter for a person rather than 사람, and 계시다 is the honorific of 있다.

example.en: In Korea, when you hand something to an elder, you offer it with both hands.

exercises.blurbEn: Join each situation to the thing you should not do.
exercises.instructionKo: 알맞은 것끼리 연결하여 한 문장으로 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Connect the phrases to make a sentence.
exercises.noteEn: Every right-hand phrase is a -지 마세요 command: the polite way to tell someone not to do something. Each is used once.

items.en: When you address an elder …
items.why: You do not call an elder by their given name. Korean reaches for a title or a kinship term instead — 선생님, 사장님, 아버님 — because a bare name puts the two of you on level terms.
items.grammar: 부르다 → 부르지 마세요. -지 마세요 attaches to the plain stem and is the polite way to tell someone not to do something.

items.en: When you receive something from a teacher …
items.why: Taking something one-handed from someone senior is casual to the point of rude. Both hands — or the right hand with the left supporting the wrist — is the respectful form. This is 두 손으로 드리다 from 연습 1 seen from the receiving side.
items.grammar: 받다 → 받지 마세요. 께 in the prompt is the honorific of 에게/한테, so the sentence has already marked the teacher as senior.

items.en: When an elder is in front of you …
items.why: Crossing your legs in front of an elder reads as relaxed and unbothered. The cue that the person present is senior is 계시다 — the honorific of 있다.
items.grammar: 앉다 → 앉지 마세요. -고 links the two actions: 다리를 꼬고 앉다 is to cross the legs and sit that way.

items.en: When you talk with a teacher …
items.why: 반말 is for close friends and people clearly younger. A teacher gets 높임말 whatever their age — the same choice 연습 1 asked about with 처음 만난 사람.
items.grammar: 하다 → 하지 마세요. Worth noticing: 하다 is irregular for 해요, but perfectly regular here — the stem 하 is untouched.

exercises.blurbEn: Name the sign that explains why B has to apologise.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 빈칸에 알맞은 것을 골라 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Complete each dialogue using the appropriate expression from the box, as in the example.
exercises.noteEn: Read A’s second sentence first: it says what cannot be done, and the sign is simply that rule as a noun.

items.en: You cannot bring food in here.
items.why: 반입 is the act of bringing something in, so 음식물 반입 금지 forbids carrying food inside — which is word for word what A’s second sentence says.
items.grammar: -을/ㄹ 수 없습니다 is "cannot": 들어오다 → 들어올 수 없습니다. And 여기는 X입니다 names a place by the rule that governs it.

lines.ko: 여기는 {}입니다. 여기에 음식을 가지고 들어올 수 없습니다.

items.en: You cannot take photographs here.
items.why: 촬영 is photographing or filming. The sign turns the banned action into a noun phrase, and A’s next sentence spells the same thing out as a verb.
items.grammar: 찍다 → 찍을 수 없습니다. Note 에서 rather than 에 — the action happens *at* the place, so 에서 marks it.

lines.ko: 여기는 {}입니다. 여기에서 사진을 찍을 수 없습니다.

items.en: You cannot make phone calls here.
items.why: The banned thing is 사용 — use. The sign forbids using the phone, not carrying it, which is why A says 전화를 할 수 없습니다 rather than anything about bringing one in.
items.grammar: 하다 → 할 수 없습니다. The sign spaces 휴대 전화; running text usually writes 휴대전화 solid.

lines.ko: 여기는 {}입니다. 여기에서 전화를 할 수 없습니다.

items.en: You cannot park a car here.
items.why: 주차 is parking. 세우다 is to bring a vehicle to a stop and leave it, so 차를 세울 수 없습니다 is the everyday way of saying the same thing the sign says formally.
items.grammar: 세우다 → 세울 수 없습니다. Four of these five signs end in 금지; 금연 is the odd one out, built as 금 (prohibit) + 연 (smoke) instead.

lines.ko: 여기는 {}입니다. 여기에 차를 세울 수 없습니다.

example.en: A: This is a no-smoking area. You cannot smoke here. — B: Oh, really? I’m sorry.

lines.ko: 여기는 {}입니다. 여기에서 담배를 피울 수 없습니다.

exercises.blurbEn: Have you ever…? Build the V-(으)ㄴ form, then answer for yourself.
exercises.instructionEn: Say it and write it, as in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The book asks you to interview a classmate. On your own, the part that can be marked is the grammar — pick the right V-(으)ㄴ form. Whether you answer 있어요 or 없어요 is your own experience, so it is kept but never marked wrong.

items.en: to go to Russia
items.why: 가- is a vowel stem, so the modifier is just ㄴ stuck onto it: 간. 가은 inserts the 으 that only consonant stems need, and 갔은 tries to stack the past-tense 았 under a form that already means past.
items.grammar: V-(으)ㄴ 적(이) 있다/없다 — to have (never) done V. Vowel stem takes -ㄴ, consonant stem takes -은.

items.en: to meet a famous person
items.why: 만나- ends in the vowel ㅏ, so ㄴ attaches directly: 만난. The same rule as 가다, and the same two traps to avoid.
items.grammar: 만나다 → 만난. 았/었 has no place in this pattern; 적이 있다 already carries the past.

items.en: to write a love letter
items.why: 쓰- is a vowel stem too, even though ㅡ looks bare: 쓴. 썼은 is the 었 past leaking in where it does not belong.
items.grammar: 쓰다 → 쓴. A ㅡ stem behaves like any other vowel stem for -(으)ㄴ.

items.en: to work a part-time job
items.why: 하- is a vowel stem: 한. 하다 is the famous irregular for 해요, but -(으)ㄴ is perfectly regular — same verb, different ending, different behaviour.
items.grammar: 하다 → 한. Worth holding next to 하다 → 해요: irregularity belongs to an ending, not to a verb.

items.en: to listen to Korean traditional music
items.why: This is the trap. 듣다 is ㄷ-irregular: before a vowel ending the ㄷ turns into ㄹ, so 듣 → 들, then -은. 듣은 keeps the ㄷ, and 든 drops the 으 that a consonant stem needs.
items.grammar: 듣다 → 들은. ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ → ㄹ before a vowel. Compare 듣고, where a consonant follows and nothing changes.

items.en: to make bulgogi
items.why: The other trap, and it pulls the opposite way. A stem ending in ㄹ drops that ㄹ before ㄴ: 만들 → 만드 + ㄴ = 만든. 만들은 keeps the ㄹ and adds 으, which is what an ordinary consonant stem would do.
items.grammar: 만들다 → 만든. ㄹ stems drop ㄹ before ㄴ, ㅂ and ㅅ. Same shape as 살다 → 산 and 알다 → 안.

example.en: I have never been to Russia.

exercises.blurbEn: Say when it happened, and get the past-tense contraction right.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The dictionary form is printed above each dialogue. Turn it into -았을/었을 때 — the same 았/었 as the plain past tense, contracting by the same rules.

items.en: I went when a friend from my home town came to Korea.
items.why: The question is about the 노래방, but the answer dates the visit by something else entirely — the friend arriving. That is what this clause is for: pinning one event to the moment another one happened.
items.grammar: 오다 → 왔을 때. ㅗ meeting 아 has nowhere to go but together: 오 + 았 = 왔. 올 때 is the same clause with no past marker at all, so it would mean whenever he comes rather than the once he did.

items.en: I realised it when the train had already pulled out.
items.why: The wallet was gone before this moment, but the knowing happened at it — and by then the train had left. -았을 때 is the tense for exactly that: the moment at which something had already finished.
items.grammar: 떠나다 → 떠났을 때. A stem ending in ㅏ absorbs the 았 rather than standing next to it: 떠나 + 았 = 떠났. 떠나았을 writes the same vowel twice.

items.en: I got angry when my friend lied to me.
items.why: 화가 나다 is something that happened to you at a particular moment, so the clause dating it has to be past as well. Note that Korean says the anger 났어요 — it arose — rather than that you were angry.
items.grammar: 하다 → 했을 때. 하 takes 여, not 았/었: 하 + 였 = 했, never 하았. It is the same 여 you already hear in 하다 → 해요.

items.en: The hardest time was when I failed the exam.
items.why: 떨어지다 is to fall, and Korean uses the same verb for failing an exam — you fall out of it. Worth holding onto: 시험에 붙다 is the other side of it, to stick, to pass.
items.grammar: 떨어지다 → 떨어졌을 때. ㅣ meeting 었 gives ㅕㅆ: 떨어지 + 었 = 떨어졌. The same contraction as 마시다 → 마셨어요 from the 어휘 pages.

items.en: I’ve liked them from the first time I saw them.
items.why: A asked 언제부터, not 언제 — from when, not when. So the answer needs 부터 on it: the point is not that you liked them at that one moment, it is that you have liked them ever since. Reading which question was actually asked is half of this item.
items.grammar: 보다 → 봤을 때, then 부터: 봤을 때부터. 때 is an ordinary noun, so 부터 attaches to it exactly as it would to any other.

example.en: A: When did you go to Jeju? — B: I went when I was little.

exercises.blurbEn: Five memories, five verbs, and five different ways the past contracts.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 문장을 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each sentence as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The book gives only a picture here and expects you to find the words yourself. The phrase is printed above each sentence so that the conjugation is what gets marked — that is the part with one right answer.

items.en: Last month, when I was ill, I wanted to go home.
items.why: Being ill is when homesickness lands hardest, and the sentence dates the wish to that. 아프다 is one of the ㅡ stems, which means the vowel it takes is decided by the syllable before the ㅡ rather than by the ㅡ itself.
items.grammar: 아프다 → 아팠을 때. The ㅡ drops before a vowel ending, and 아프 looks back at its ㅏ to pick 아: 아프 + 아 = 아파, then 았을 때. 아프었을 keeps the ㅡ and takes the wrong vowel on top of it.

items.en: I was really happy when I got the prize at the last graduation ceremony.
items.why: 수료식 is the ceremony that closes a course, and the prize changes hands at one moment inside it. 받다 is a plain consonant stem, so nothing contracts here — the only decision is which vowel the ending takes.
items.grammar: 받다 → 받았을 때. Vowel harmony settles it: a stem whose vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ takes 았, everything else takes 었. 받 has ㅏ, so 받았을, not 받었을.

items.en: The saddest time was when my grandmother passed away.
items.why: 돌아가시다 is how Korean says that someone has died, and the 시 inside it is not decoration — it is the honorific, and it is the entire reason the word is a respectful one. 돌아갔을 때 is the same verb with the 시 taken out, and means she went back somewhere.
items.grammar: 돌아가시다 → 돌아가셨을 때. 시 + 었 → 셨, the ordinary ㅣ contraction. 돌아가실 때 is future or general, which is not what a memory is.

lines.ko: 어제 지갑을 {} 친구가 같이 찾아 줬어요.

items.en: When I lost my wallet yesterday, a friend helped me look for it.
items.why: 잃어버리다 is 잃다 with -어 버리다 stuck on, which adds the sense that the thing is gone and not coming back on its own. Only the last piece conjugates, so the verb behaves like any ㅣ stem.
items.grammar: 잃어버리다 → 잃어버렸을 때. 버리 + 었 = 버렸. Worth noticing 찾아 줬어요 as well: -아/어 주다 is doing something for someone, so the friend did the searching on your behalf.

items.en: When I was little I played a lot of football with my friends.
items.why: 어리다 is to be young and 어렵다 is to be difficult — two verbs that look like one until you conjugate them. 어려웠을 때 is the second one, and it turns this into playing football when life was hard.
items.grammar: 어리다 → 어렸을 때. 어리 + 었 = 어렸. 어릴 때 is idiomatic Korean for the same idea and you will hear it constantly, but this exercise is drilling -았을/었을 때 and the book’s key prints 어렸을 때.

example.en: The phone rang when I got home.

exercises.blurbEn: Ask whether it is allowed, then answer that it is not — both halves.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: Two blanks per sign. A asks with -아/어도 돼요 — may I — and B refuses with -(으)면 안 돼요. One verb, two endings, and they attach by different rules: -아/어도 needs the 해요-form vowel, -(으)면 goes straight onto the plain stem.

items.en: A: May I make a phone call here? — B: No, you may not make calls here.
items.why: The trap on A’s side is 하면 돼요, which is a real pattern but a different one: -(으)면 되다 means it will do if you do, whereas -아/어도 되다 asks whether it is permitted. On B’s side, -(으)면 attaches to the plain stem 하, never to the 해요 form.
items.grammar: 하다 → 해도 돼요 / 하면 안 돼요. 하 + 여도 = 해도, and 하 + 면 = 하면. 하지 안 돼요 is 하지 마세요 and 안 되다 crossed with each other; -지 goes with 마세요 or 않다, not with 안 되다.

items.en: A: May I eat here? — B: No, you may not eat here.
items.why: This is the 음식물 반입 금지 sign from 어휘 연습 3, seen from the other side: there the rule was a noun, here it is a verb aimed at you. 먹 ends in a consonant, which is what decides both endings.
items.grammar: 먹다 → 먹어도 돼요 / 먹으면 안 돼요. The stem vowel ㅓ takes 어, not 아. And a consonant-final stem needs the 으 in -으면 — 먹면 is what the rule exists to prevent.

items.en: A: May I take photographs here? — B: No, you may not take photographs here.
items.why: 찍다 has ㅣ in the stem, and ㅣ is not one of the two vowels that take 아 — so 어, the same as 먹다. Museums and 공연장 are where you will actually be asked this.
items.grammar: 찍다 → 찍어도 돼요 / 찍으면 안 돼요. Only ㅏ and ㅗ stems take 아; everything else, ㅣ included, takes 어. And 찍 ends in a consonant, so -으면 keeps its 으.

items.en: A: May I smoke here? — B: No, you may not smoke here.
items.why: This is 금연 from 어휘 연습 3 put into a verb. 피우다 pulls in two directions at once, which is what makes it the useful item here: the -아/어도 half contracts and the -(으)면 half does not.
items.grammar: 피우다 → 피워도 돼요 / 피우면 안 돼요. ㅜ + 어 → ㅝ, so 피우 + 어도 = 피워도. But 피우 ends in a vowel, so -면 goes on bare: 피우으면 is the 으 that only consonant stems need.

items.en: A: May I swim here? — B: No, you may not swim here.
items.why: Same verb as item 1, so the trap moved: it is now the spelling of 되다 itself. 되 + 어요 contracts to 돼요, and 되요 is the single most common misspelling in Korean — native writers get it wrong too.
items.grammar: 하다 → 해도 돼요 / 하면 안 돼요. 되다 conjugates like any other verb: 되 + 어요 = 돼요. The test native writers use is to try 하/해 in the same slot: if 해 fits, write 돼 — 안 해요 works, so it is 안 돼요 — and if 하 fits, write 되, as in 되세요.

example.en: A: May I park a car here? — B: No, you may not park here.

exercises.blurbEn: Read the reply first, then ask the question it answers.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: Here the prohibition is the question: A asks -(으)면 안 돼요, meaning is it really not allowed. B’s answer is already printed, so read it first — it tells you which way the question has to point, and in item 4 it tells you how politely to ask.

items.en: A: When I present, may I not read from my script? — B: Right, you have to memorise it all.
items.why: B says you have to memorise it, so A must be asking whether the script is off limits — 하면 안 돼요, not 하면 돼요, which would be asking whether reading it is fine. -(으)면서 in the prompt is two things at once: looking at the script while presenting.
items.grammar: 하다 → 하면 안 돼요. -(으)면 attaches to the plain stem 하, so 해면 is the 해요 form leaking into a place that does not take it.

items.en: A: I don’t feel like doing it now — can’t I do it later? — B: No. Do it now.
items.why: -는데 is the little hinge A leans on: it lays out the situation and then asks for something because of it. B answers in 반말, so these two are close — but A is still asking upward, which is why the question keeps 요.
items.grammar: 하다 → 하면 안 돼요. Two traps: 되요 for 돼요, which is 되 + 어요 uncontracted and simply wrong; and 했으면, which puts the past tense where -(으)면 안 되다 takes a plain stem.

items.en: A: The medicine is so bitter — can’t I leave just a little? — B: No. You have to take it all.
items.why: 남기다 is to leave something behind, so 조금만 남기다 is leaving a little in the cup. Medicine in Korean is 먹다, eaten rather than taken. One thing to know: the book’s answer key prints 안 먹으면 안 돼요 for this item, which is good Korean and fits B’s reply, but it is not built from 조금만 남기다 — the phrase printed under the picture. This page follows the picture.
items.grammar: 남기다 → 남기면 안 돼요. 남기 ends in a vowel, so -면 goes on bare; the 으 in 남기으면 is the one only consonant stems need. Compare 먹으면 in 연습 1, where the stem does end in a consonant.

items.en: A: 언니, can I wear this tomorrow? — B: Sure, go ahead.
items.why: This is the only 반말 exchange on the page, and the two words that give it away are 언니 and B’s 입어도 돼 with no 요 on it. Between sisters the 요 comes off, so 안 돼요 would be oddly formal here — right grammar, wrong distance.
items.grammar: 입다 → 입으면 안 돼. 입 ends in a consonant, so -으면 keeps its 으. Dropping the 요 from 안 돼요 is all 반말 takes here.

example.en: A: May I not go outside now? — B: No. Go out once the exam is over.

exercises.blurbEn: Turn "you have to" into "not doing it will not do" — twice negative, same meaning.
exercises.instructionEn: Rewrite the sentences as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: 꼭 해야 돼요 and 안 하면 안 돼요 say the same thing from opposite ends: one says you must, the other says that not doing it will not do. Both negatives have to be there — drop either one and the sentence means the opposite.

items.en: I have to get the homework done by tomorrow. → Not doing it by tomorrow will not do.
items.why: This is the whole point of the exercise, and 하면 안 돼요 is the sentence that proves it: with only one negative it says you must not do the homework, which is the opposite of what was asked. The obligation lives in the pair of negatives, not in either one.
items.grammar: 해야 돼요 → 안 하면 안 돼요. 안 goes in front of the verb, and -(으)면 안 되다 goes on the plain stem, so the past tense in 안 했으면 has nowhere to attach.

items.en: I have to give up smoking. → Not giving it up will not do.
items.why: 끊다 is to cut or sever, and Korean uses it for quitting a habit — you cut it off. It is the same verb you use for hanging up a phone call, 전화를 끊다.
items.grammar: 끊어야 돼요 → 안 끊으면 안 돼요. The stem 끊 ends in a consonant cluster, so -으면 keeps its 으 as it would after any consonant.

items.en: I have to be at school by nine in the morning. → Not being there by nine will not do.
items.why: 까지 is the deadline marker — up to and no later. Paired with 안 …면 안 돼요 it becomes the way Korean states a rule you cannot slip past.
items.grammar: 가야 돼요 → 안 가면 안 돼요. 가 ends in a vowel, so -면 goes on bare: 안 가으면 borrows the 으 that 끊으면 needs and 가면 does not.

items.en: I have to take delivery of the parcel today. → Missing it today will not do.
items.why: This is the one item in the set that takes 못 rather than 안, and the difference is choice. 안 받으면 is refusing the parcel; 못 받으면 is failing to be there for it, which is the thing that actually goes wrong. A parcel is not something you decline.
items.grammar: 받아야 해요 → 못 받으면 안 돼요. 안 is chosen not to, 못 is unable to, and both sit in front of the verb. Note the prompt ends 해야 해요 rather than 해야 돼요 — 되다 and 하다 are interchangeable in that pattern.

example.en: I really have to exercise. → Not exercising will not do.

exercises.blurbEn: The teacher asks if it is your first time. It is not.
exercises.noteEn: In the book this is the listening drill on track 10: the teacher asks, you answer out loud, one after another. The pattern never changes — 아니요, 전에 …-(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 — so the only thing to get right is the modifier, and the four verbs are picked to cover all three ways it forms. Use the speaker button: say it before you read it.

items.en: T: Is this your first time seeing this film? — S: No, I’ve seen it before.
items.why: 처음 봐요? asks whether this is the first time, so 아니요 commits you to there having been an earlier one — which is exactly what -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 records. 전에 pins that earlier time to somewhere before now without saying when.
items.grammar: 보다 → 본. A vowel stem takes the bare ㄴ. 봤은 stacks the past 았 under a form that already means past, and 적이 있다 carries the pastness by itself.

items.en: T: Is this your first time eating this dish? — S: No, I’ve eaten it before.
items.why: The first consonant stem in the drill, and that is why it is here. 먹 ends in ㄱ, so the ending needs its 으 to be sayable at all — the same 으 that 보다 had no use for.
items.grammar: 먹다 → 먹은. Consonant stem takes -은, vowel stem takes -ㄴ. 먹는 is the present modifier — 먹는 사람 is the person who is eating — and it cannot stand in front of 적이 있다.

items.en: T: Is this your first time meeting Michael? — S: No, I’ve met him before.
items.why: 만나다 ends in ㅏ, so it goes the way 보다 went and not the way 먹다 did. 씨 after a name is the everyday polite way to refer to someone who is not senior to you — a teacher would get 선생님 instead.
items.grammar: 만나다 → 만난. Vowel stem, so -ㄴ attaches straight on. Both wrong answers here are the two mistakes already seen: the present modifier, and the past put in twice.

items.en: T: Is this your first time hearing this song? — S: No, I’ve heard it before.
items.why: The one the drill builds towards, and the teacher gives it away in the question: 들어요, not 듣어요. The ㄷ has already turned into ㄹ there for the same reason it does here.
items.grammar: 듣다 → 들은. ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending, then the consonant-stem -은 goes on. Compare 듣고, where a consonant follows and the ㄷ stays as it is.

example.en: T: Is this your first time going to Gyeongju? — S: No, I’ve been before.

exercises.blurbEn: When were you happiest? Date the answer to the moment.
exercises.noteEn: The bracket under each question is the phrase to build the clause from — the same cue the book prints. Every answer ends by echoing the teacher’s own verb, so the only thing you supply is the 때 clause in front of it.

items.en: T: When were you happiest? — S: When I got the scholarship.
items.why: 장학금 is a scholarship, and 받다 is the same verb the 문법과 표현 page used for 상을 받다. The answer repeats 제일 기뻤어요 from the question, which is what makes these drills quick to say out loud.
items.grammar: 받다 → 받았을 때. The stem vowel is ㅏ, so the ending is 았, not 었. 받을 때 drops the past entirely and would mean whenever you receive one.

items.en: T: When were you saddest? — S: When my grandmother passed away.
items.why: The same sentence the 문법과 표현 page asked for, now said against the clock. 돌아가시다 keeps its 시 because that is the honorific, and taking it out leaves 돌아가다 — she went back somewhere.
items.grammar: 돌아가시다 → 돌아가셨을 때. 시 + 었 → 셨. Note 슬펐어요 in the question as well: 슬프다 is a ㅡ stem, so 슬프 + 어 → 슬퍼, then 었.

items.en: T: When did you hear that story? — S: When I went back to my home town.
items.why: You heard it on a trip home, so the clause dates the hearing to that visit. 이야기를 듣다 is how Korean says to hear a story — 이야기 covers both the story and the telling of it.
items.grammar: 가다 → 갔을 때. ㅏ meeting 았 leaves one syllable: 가 + 았 = 갔. 가았을 writes the vowel twice, which is the mistake this stem invites.

items.en: T: When did you get Nana’s call? — S: When I got home.
items.why: This is the sentence the 문법과 표현 연습 2 example was built on, turned round: there the phone rang as you arrived, here you answer for when the call came. 전화를 받다 is to take a call, the same 받다 as item 1.
items.grammar: 도착하다 → 도착했을 때. Every 하다 verb goes 하 + 였 → 했, so 도착하았을 is wrong twice over — wrong vowel, and uncontracted.

example.en: T: When did you see that film? — S: I saw it when I was little.

exercises.blurbEn: Turn the teacher’s bare phrase into a request for permission.
exercises.instructionEn: Ask the question, as in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The other half of the pair, and the one the workbook pages skip: -아/어도 되다 is asking whether something is allowed. The teacher gives the plain phrase and you put the ending on it, which means finding the 해요-form vowel first — that is where all four of these differ.

items.en: T: go out now — S: May I go out now?
items.why: The trap that is not a spelling one: 나가면 돼요 is real Korean but a different question. -(으)면 되다 asks whether doing it would be enough; -아/어도 되다 asks whether you are allowed to.
items.grammar: 나가다 → 나가도 돼요. The stem ends in ㅏ and the ending starts with 아, so they merge into one: 나가 + 아도 = 나가도, never 나가아도.

items.en: T: call at night — S: May I call at night?
items.why: Ringing someone late is exactly the kind of thing this pattern is for. 전화하다 is a 하다 verb like hundreds of others, so getting it right here gets all of them right.
items.grammar: 전화하다 → 전화해도 돼요. 하 takes 여, not 아/어: 하 + 여도 = 해도. 전화하도 leaves the vowel out altogether and there is nothing for -도 to attach to.

items.en: T: use this computer — S: May I use this computer?
items.why: 쓰다 is the ㅡ stem of the set, and it is a busy verb: to write, to use, and to wear on the head. All three senses conjugate the same way.
items.grammar: 쓰다 → 써도 돼요. The ㅡ drops before a vowel ending and there is no syllable before it to take the vowel from, so it defaults to 어: 쓰 + 어 = 써.

items.en: T: eat here — S: May I eat here?
items.why: The same question the 문법과 표현 sign page asked, and the answer it expects there is 먹으면 안 돼요. Asking and refusing are the two halves the book keeps putting side by side.
items.grammar: 먹다 → 먹어도 돼요. The stem vowel is ㅓ, so the ending is 어. Only ㅏ and ㅗ stems take 아.

example.en: T: take photographs here — S: May I take photographs here?

exercises.blurbEn: Refuse the permission the teacher just asked for.
exercises.noteEn: The reply to 연습 3. The teacher asks with the ending that contracts and you answer with the one that does not — -(으)면 goes on the plain stem, so a verb can look irregular in the question and perfectly regular in the answer. Item 4 is where that bites.

items.en: T: May I park here? — S: No, you may not park here.
items.why: 주차 금지 from 어휘 연습 3, said to a person instead of printed on a sign. The teacher’s 주차해도 has the 해 in it, which is exactly what makes 주차해면 tempting.
items.grammar: 주차하다 → 주차하면 안 돼요. -(으)면 goes on the plain stem 하, so the 해 that -아/어도 needed has no business here. And 하 ends in a vowel, so no 으.

items.en: T: May I smoke here? — S: No, you may not smoke here.
items.why: The question says 피워, the answer says 피우, and both are right. ㅜ + 어 → ㅝ only happens when a vowel follows, and -면 is a consonant.
items.grammar: 피우다 → 피우면 안 돼요. Vowel-final stem, so plain -면. 피우으면 borrows the 으 that only consonant stems need.

items.en: T: May I drink a soft drink here? — S: No, you may not drink here.
items.why: 음료수 is a soft drink rather than a drink in general — 마실 것 or 음료 covers that. 마시다 is the same verb 어휘 연습 1 conjugated for drinking with elders.
items.grammar: 마시다 → 마시면 안 돼요. The 셔 in the teacher’s 마셔도 is ㅣ + 어 contracting; nothing contracts before -면, so the stem comes back as 마시.

items.en: T: May I sing here? — S: No, you may not sing here.
items.why: The best item in the drill. 부르다 is 르-irregular, and the teacher shows it off: 부르 + 어 doubles the ㄹ and gives 불러. Then the answer needs -면, no vowel follows, and the verb goes straight back to being ordinary.
items.grammar: 부르다 → 부르면 안 돼요. 르-irregular verbs are only irregular before a vowel. 불러면 carries the irregular form into a place that never triggers it — the single most useful mistake to stop making.

example.en: T: May I take photographs here? — S: No, you may not take photographs.
